analysis.one_liner: Adds Medicare bonus payments for emergency care and shifts malpractice claims for uninsured ER patients to the federal government.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a Democrat and co-introduced by a Republican with 47 bipartisan cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote in the House and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill responds to strain on hospital emergency departments, which by law must treat everyone who arrives regardless of ability to pay. It would treat hospitals, emergency rooms, and doctors who provide emergency care to uninsured people as federal employees for malpractice purposes, meaning lawsuits over that care would be brought against the federal government under federal rules and paid from a federally funded pool. It would also add a 10 percent Medicare payment bonus for physicians working in emergency departments and offer hospitals an extra 10 percent if they meet federal standards for promptly moving emergency patients into hospital beds.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospitals and emergency physicians gain the most directly: they get a 10 percent Medicare payment boost, a chance at 10 percent hospital incentive payments, and protection from traditional malpractice suits when treating uninsured emergency patients. Uninsured patients benefit indirectly, since the bill aims to keep financially strained emergency departments open and reduce overcrowding so care remains available.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals, emergency departments, and physicians treating uninsured emergency patients would be deemed employees of the Public Health Service, so malpractice claims over that care would be handled as federal claims supported by a separate federal fund.

Physicians would receive an additional Medicare payment equal to 10 percent of the normal amount for services furnished in a hospital emergency department, intended to keep specialists willing to cover emergency care.

Hospitals that certify they meet federal standards for promptly admitting emergency patients who need inpatient beds would receive an extra 10 percent payment on emergency department visits, aimed at reducing overcrowding and patients boarded in hallways.
The bill pairs the money with enforcement: civil monetary penalties for filing a false certification and for a pattern of failing the prompt-admission standards, plus audits and a complaint process.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the cost twice: the physician and hospital bonuses are paid out of the Medicare Part B trust fund with no offsetting cuts or revenue, and the malpractice claim fund is financed by annual appropriations, with payments capped at whatever Congress provides. People injured by negligent emergency care while uninsured would give up their ordinary malpractice remedy and be limited to a federal claim from that capped fund.

drawbacks.text: Patients harmed by negligent emergency care while uninsured would no longer sue the hospital or doctor in the ordinary way; their claims would become federal claims against the government, which is a narrower and generally less generous path.

The malpractice fund is capped at the amount Congress appropriates each year; if claims exceed that amount, the bill directs the Secretary to limit payments, leaving some injured patients without full compensation.
The 10 percent physician bonus is paid from the Medicare Part B trust fund with no offsetting spending cuts or new revenue, adding to Medicare's costs.

The hospital incentive pays facilities an extra 10 percent for meeting standards for prompt admissions, meaning taxpayers pay hospitals more to do what patient-safety advocates argue they should be doing already; the bill does include audits and penalties for hospitals that certify falsely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real problem: emergency departments must treat uninsured patients under federal law, and many are financially strained, so keeping specialists available and beds flowing matters to everyone. But its design leans toward providers. The headline benefits for ordinary people — kept-open emergency rooms and shorter waits — are indirect, while the direct gains of extra Medicare money and a malpractice shield go to hospitals and physicians, and the trade-off is borne by taxpayers and by patients who lose the ordinary right to sue over negligent care. A version that funded the bonuses with offsets and preserved stronger patient remedies would have balanced the interests better.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bart Gordon, a Democrat from Tennessee, introduced the bill on September 22, 2005, together with Rep. Pete Sessions, a Republican from Texas.
It was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, a split referral that gives either committee the power to hold the bill.
In early October 2005 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote after that.
The bill had 47 cosponsors, 23 Republicans and 24 Democrats, when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, without the bill ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and emergency physicians lost the chance at new federal payments and a malpractice shield. Taxpayers were spared the added Medicare and appropriations costs, and people injured by emergency-room negligence kept their full right to sue.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly even across parties: 23 Republican and 24 Democratic cosponsors, with the bill co-introduced by one member of each party; no opposition vote ever occurred because it never reached the floor.

industries.note: Hospitals would gain a 10 percent incentive payment for meeting prompt-admission standards and a malpractice shield for emergency care of uninsured patients. The shield weakens remedies for patients harmed by negligent care, while the payments and access goal align with keeping emergency rooms open to the public.

Emergency doctors would receive a 10 percent Medicare payment bonus for emergency department work and would be treated as federal employees for malpractice claims tied to uninsured patients, lowering their liability risk. The trade-off for patients is a narrower path to compensation after medical errors.

industries.industry: Medical malpractice plaintiffs and their attorneys
industries.note: Claims arising from emergency care of uninsured patients would move into the federal system against the government, with payments limited to an annually appropriated fund. That reduces both the practical reach and the potential recovery of malpractice claims.
